item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Not gonna lie, guys. I wrote this in about fifteen minutes. I fully accept these criticisms and agree.

Actually, let me elaborate on my thought process for this one, as I dislike using "not much time" as an excuse. This was largely cold posted, with only Moose making any comments for grammar, and no real content changes to be had.

I could have gone in to detail about the actual method of capture, but I really prefer that be left up to the imagination. Yes, a scope is mentioned and a gun implied, and I hoped that the question of if he was dead or alive when he got to Mann was extremely vague, since the Foundation grabbed him immediately, and Mann has a noted penchant for vivisection, there's lots and lots of room for the implication. Spelling it out wasn't satisfying to me, and I doubt that it would have been satisfying to readers. If it's "Yes, he's dead," then the problem of "why would they kill him, that's retarded" arises. If he's alive, then it's squick for squick's sake, and I don't care for that either. It's a cat box, guys. Sorry.

As for why we didn't just wait and bag him at home… Hell. We probably could have. But at the same time, we're not sure what this guy does or how his powers work. Really, if he's got Bright's fucking email address… Who knows.

As for notes about the letter being annoying, I agree, but I didn't want to change it. Authorial intent.

One thing to note:

Troy and Echo talk about Chicken McNuggets.

See, that's where you're wrong. That's not Troy and Echo. That's Lament and Dodridge. If you're not separating them, then you're not getting the character relationship there. I am not Lament. There's a reason I almost always call him Lament instead of Troy in the context of tales, and it's to avoid the Dr. Bright/Dr. Bright or Dr. Clef/Dr. Clef problem.

item.content:encoded:
There is a lot of wiggle room in that last paragraph break. That line could represent a long time and a lot of action.
Johnny Not-So-Swift could have spent many unpleasant days being interrogated about the sources of his semi-accurate intel. Followed by an even less pleasant period of testing and assesment. At some point, he ceased to be a living sample. Accidents happen, staff get over-enthusiastic with their "persuasion". Especially when the subject is an annoying twit like Johnny. Time to salvage what data we can with an old-fashioned autopsy.

There is some in-story evidence to support this. Dodridge was using a weapon that was large enough for a scope, but quite enough that bystanders didn't hear a shot. Tranquilizer rifles are nearly silent; and the right drugs can drop a man so fast he (or anyone watching) won't know what happened.

Edit: Forgot to mention, I enjoyed it.
